subtopic: Friendship betrayal to reconciliation or ending
passage:
"Aadhya and Ira, the twins," people call us. They ask how we stayed close for six years at the same firm. Honestly? We started on the same day, both terrified, both given the desks next to the broken AC. That was the beginning.
When my engagement broke, Ira drove to my flat at midnight with a box of jalebis and didn't ask a single question until I was ready. When her father was in hospital in Lucknow for three weeks, I covered her client calls and sent her updates so she wouldn't miss anything.
There's a kind of friend you perform for, and a kind you don't. With Ira, I've been the girl crying in the office washroom with mascara everywhere, and she just handed me tissues and said, "Fix your face, we have a meeting in ten, you'll be brilliant."
She's the one person I can be a complete mess around. I don't have to explain myself.

qa.q: What did Ira bring when Aadhya's engagement broke?
qa.a: Ira drove to Aadhya's flat at midnight with a box of jalebis.

qa.q: Why does Aadhya say she doesn't have to explain herself with Ira?
qa.a: Aadhya feels completely safe with Ira: she can be a mess, even crying in the washroom, and Ira meets it with care, not judgement. 😊

qa.q: What habits have kept this friendship strong?
qa.a: Each shows up at the other's worst moments in practical ways, like covering calls or arriving at midnight, and neither asks the other to perform.

qa.q: What might Ira value about the friendship?
qa.a: Ira probably values that Aadhya carried her work while her father was in hospital, so she could be with family without worrying.

grounding: Shows two colleagues who started together and carried each other through a broken engagement and a parent's illness, with one able to be at her weakest without judgement.

subtopic: Friendship betrayal to reconciliation or ending
passage:
I sit two desks away from Sarita and Vijay in the accounts team, so I've watched them for three years. They joined the same week, fresh from college, and they still order lunch from the same dhaba every Thursday.
Last winter, when Sarita's mother was ill, Vijay quietly took over her month-end files and never mentioned it in team meetings. When Vijay's girlfriend ended things, Sarita sat with him on the stairwell for most of an afternoon.
What I notice most is how different Sarita is around him. With the rest of us she's polished, careful with every word. With Vijay she'll put her head on the desk and groan, "I'm useless today," and he'll slide a chai across and say, "Useless people don't finish audits." She laughs.
I can't know what's in their heads. But she looks like someone who knows she won't be judged.

qa.q: What does Vijay slide across when Sarita says she's useless?
qa.a: Vijay slides a chai across and says, 'Useless people don't finish audits.'

qa.q: What does Sarita's change around Vijay suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests Sarita feels safe with Vijay; she drops her polished, careful manner because she trusts she won't be judged. 🙂

qa.q: What could the rest of the team learn from how these two support each other?
qa.a: Quiet, practical help, like taking over files without announcing it, builds deep trust more than big words do.

qa.q: How does the narrator see Sarita differently with Vijay than with everyone else?
qa.a: The narrator sees a polished, careful Sarita with the team and a relaxed, honest one with Vijay, while admitting not knowing what either of them thinks.

grounding: Illustrates, through a colleague's eyes, a years-long work friendship through illness and breakup in which one woman can be at her weakest without being judged.
